steps.action:
# The Last Light

Maren had kept the light for eleven years before she stopped counting.

The mainland people always asked the same question when the supply boat came — *don't you get lonely out there?* — and she always gave them the same smile that meant *you wouldn't understand*, which was true, and also kind.

The light didn't need her the way it used to. There were automated systems now, backups for the backups, little green LED indicators that blinked their quiet reassurances to no one. The maritime authority had told her this politely, in a letter, twice. She had filed both letters in the drawer beneath the foghorn switch and gone back to her rounds.

What she didn't tell the mainland people was this: she wasn't keeping the light for the ships anymore. She was keeping it for the moment just before dawn, when the beam swept across the water and caught the surface at precisely the angle that made the whole ocean look like something that had never heard of trouble. Four seconds of that. Every single morning.

She'd tried to explain it once to her sister, who lived in the city and had a good job and worried about Maren with a devotion that was exhausting and dear.

*It sounds like you're hiding*, her sister had said.

*I'm not hiding*, Maren had answered. *I'm the most visible thing for forty miles.*

Her sister had laughed despite herself, which was exactly what Maren had intended.

In November, a young man arrived on the supply boat looking pale and official. He had the letter — a third letter, more formal than the others — and a kind face that made the whole thing worse. He explained about the automation, about budget cycles, about thanking her for her service, and he stood in her kitchen drinking the tea she'd made him because she'd been raised right, even out here.

When he left, she walked up the hundred and twelve steps — she knew them all, the creaky one at sixty-seven, the cold draft at ninety — and she stood beside the great rotating lamp.

She thought about the ships she had guided. The ones she'd never see, never know. The captain somewhere out there who had seen this light through a storm and had maybe not even registered it consciously, just felt the quiet correction of course, the small adjustment that carries you home.

It seemed like enough.

More than enough, actually.

She turned off the light herself, before they could do it for her. She stood in the sudden dark, watched the beam from the automated system blink on three seconds later, cold and precise and perfect.

Then she went downstairs and started packing, slowly, the way a person does when they're not quite ready but have decided to be brave about it.

She left the two letters in the drawer. She took the view.
